title: Efficient learning of well-separated Gaussian mixtures
formal: Is there an end-to-end polynomial-time, polynomial-sample algorithm for learning the parameters of well-separated spherical Gaussian mixtures at the source’s square-root-logarithmic separation scale? More precisely, do there exist one uniform randomized learner \(A\) and universal constants \(C_{\rm sep},B,a\ge1\) such that the following holds for every integer \(k\ge3\), \(d\ge1\), \(s\ge k\), \(R\ge1\), \(t\ge3\)? For every mixture \[P=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\pi_i N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2 I_d),\qquad \pi_i\ge1/s,\quad \frac{\max_i\sigma_i}{\min_i\sigma_i}\le R,\] whose means satisfy \[\|\mu_i-\mu_j\|_2\ge C_{\rm sep}\max\{\sigma_i,\sigma_j\}\sqrt{\log(sR)}\quad(i\ne j),\] the learner, given only \(d,k,s,R,t\) and independent unlabeled samples from \(P\), returns \(k\) estimated component parameters with probability at least \(2/3\) for which some permutation \(\tau\) of \([k]\) satisfies, for every \(i\), \[\frac{|\widehat\pi_{\tau(i)}-\pi_i|}{\pi_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{\|\widehat\mu_{\tau(i)}-\mu_i\|_2}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1t,\qquad \frac{|\widehat\sigma_{\tau(i)}-\sigma_i|}{\sigma_i}\le\frac1{t\sqrt d}.\] Require at most \(B(d+k+s+R+t)^a\) samples and total arithmetic operations, including output. The learner receives no initial estimates of the means, weights or variances. It need not attain the source’s sharper near-linear sample bound; the selected question asks for polynomial sample complexity and polynomial time simultaneously.
why: Identifiable clusters need not be easy to locate. This problem asks whether the separation that makes parameter recovery statistically feasible also permits an efficient global algorithm. It is a basic test of the computational cost of fitting latent-variable models when the number of components grows.
status_note: The source’s selected §4.3 question concerns a global polynomial-time algorithm at square-root-logarithmic separation, while Theorem9 supplies the parameter metric and a statistically efficient but potentially inefficient procedure. The strongest directly checked later polynomial-time identity-covariance result uses log^{1/2+c}(k) separation with fixed c>0. Low-dimensional Fourier results, the 2026 slow-characteristic-function family excluding Gaussians, and newer nonspherical clustering bounds do not match the full target. No matching resolution was found in this bounded review through 16 September 2026; current status remains uncertain rather than a proved assertion of openness. The public bound parameters and exact-real arithmetic convention are explicit and are not claimed equivalent to a finite-bit interface.

progress.text: The source proves local EM convergence and sample-efficient parameter learning, while explicitly leaving global polynomial-time initialization unresolved.
Polynomial time becomes possible for identity-covariance mixtures at log^{1/2+c}(k) separation for every fixed positive c.
Fourier methods improve the separation threshold in low dimensions, with parameter-dependent runtime outside that regime.
A new sparse-Fourier algorithm handles a slow-decay distribution family excluding Gaussians; its mixed-family extension has additional conditions.
New nonspherical clustering algorithms improve dimension dependence while retaining nonpolynomial component/weight dependence.

importance.reason: A central unresolved efficiency threshold for spherical mixture parameter learning, with a clear separation between global initialization and statistically efficient local refinement.

sentences: The card asks for globally learning well-separated spherical Gaussian mixtures with both polynomial samples and polynomial computation.
The weights, centers and unequal component scales are hidden, and all must be recovered to the source’s stated relative accuracy up to one permutation.
The source’s efficient local refinement requires initialization that its sample-efficient procedure does not find in polynomial time.
Later algorithms improve separation or dimension dependence but retain assumptions or parameter costs that do not meet the full target.
A Lean resolution must establish or refute one uniform end-to-end learner under the explicit separation, access and arithmetic-cost conventions.

definitions:
Here \(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_k>0\) sum to one, \(\mu_i\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(\sigma_i>0\). The covariance matrix of component \(i\) is \(\sigma_i^2 I_d\), so \(\sigma_i\) is a standard deviation, not a variance. To draw an observation, select an index with probabilities \(\pi_i\) and then draw from that component; the index is never revealed. Different observations and learner coins are independent. Each component’s coordinates have independent variance \(\sigma_i^2\), but both its center and scale are unknown. Weights need not be equal and scales need not coincide. There is no bound on the absolute centers or on the common absolute scale, no general-position or linear-independence assumption on centers, and no target-specific advice.

\([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(I_d\) is the identity matrix and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_j v_j^2)^{1/2}\). The logarithm is natural. The same constant \(C_{\rm sep}\) applies to every instance and is independent of requested accuracy. In the balanced equal-scale special case \(s=k,R=1\), the separation is a constant times \(\sqrt{\log k}\) standard deviations. For general mixtures, the source’s separation (14) uses \(\sqrt{\log(\rho_\sigma/\pi_{\min})}\), where \(\rho_\sigma=\max_i\sigma_i/\min_i\sigma_i\) and \(\pi_{\min}=\min_i\pi_i\). The public integers \(s,R\) are conservative bounds on \(1/\pi_{\min}\) and \(\rho_\sigma\); the displayed separation is imposed with those supplied bounds. Rounding each true quantity upward increases it by at most a factor of two, absorbed by the universal separation constant. This is an explicit public-parameter convention for the source’s polynomial-resource question, not a restriction to balanced or known-variance mixtures.

All five integer parameters are supplied in unary. Accuracy is \(\varepsilon=1/t\); these reciprocal tolerances express arbitrary precision within a constant factor. The output is a finite list \((\widehat\pi_i,\widehat\mu_i,\widehat\sigma_i)_{i=1}^k\) with positive estimated scales, nonnegative weights summing to one, and real mean vectors. Its component order is immaterial: the same permutation must match all three parameter types. The loss is parameter recovery in the displayed relative/scaled units. Merely producing a distribution close in total variation, a good partition for some observations, or a sampler with a different representation does not by itself meet this output requirement.

Use a finite uniform exact-real register program, with rational constants in its fixed code. Copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division guarded at zero, comparison, branching, square root of a nonnegative number, and each random fair bit cost one operation. Integer control, input reading, register access and writing each output real are counted. Loading a \(d\)-coordinate observation costs \(d\) operations. The program has no component-label oracle, chosen-input density oracle, exact-moment oracle, free optimization procedure, floor/digit extraction or arbitrary real advice. Its single polynomial bound must hold for every target, sample history and coin history; the success guarantee accounts for the randomness. Constants, program and polynomial exponent are common to all parameters. The source does not specify coordinate-bit precision; this declared real-arithmetic convention does not assert an equivalent finite-bit algorithm. Any finite-precision version needs its own sample representation and justified rounding/error analysis.

The time bound explicitly allows polynomial dependence on the weight and scale-ratio bounds, while the separation depends on their logarithm. It is not polynomial time if the exponent on dimension or component count grows with \(k\), \(t\), or a separation parameter. A family of algorithms at separation \(\log^{1/2+c}k\) with constants or exponents depending on a fixed \(c>0\) does not imply a single algorithm at \(c=0\).
answer_criterion: Give a Lean proof of the uniform existence proposition or its negation. A positive proof must include global initialization from unlabeled samples, every component’s mean/weight/scale guarantee under one permutation, the stated success probability, and a universal polynomial bound for samples and all arithmetic/output costs. A local convergence theorem with accurate starting parameters is not enough. A negative result must rule out every learner and universal constants for some allowed parameters and mixture, rather than merely a particular iterative method. A computational assumption must remain a hypothesis unless proved. Larger asymptotic separation, fixed component count, equal variances only, or a weaker distribution-learning output is not a complete answer. The requested parameter accuracy is explicitly \(1/t\), with the dimension factor in the standard-deviation error retained.

source_formulation.text: At the well-separated spherical-Gaussian regime of the paper, can parameter learning from unlabeled samples use both polynomial time and polynomial sample complexity?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: Expectation maximization alternates between estimating component membership probabilities and updating parameters. The source proves strong local refinement guarantees and an information-theoretically sample-efficient initialization. The latter can be computationally expensive, which is why its final initialization discussion still asks for an end-to-end polynomial algorithm.

The source permits unknown unequal spherical variances and unequal weights. Its Theorem 9 measures mean error in units of each component’s standard deviation and asks for a smaller relative scale error as dimension grows. The completed statement preserves those parameter guarantees, rather than replacing them with a total-variation approximation or clustering-only task.

Li–Liu obtain polynomial-time learning for identity-covariance mixtures when separation is \(\Omega(\log^{1/2+c}k)\) for any fixed \(c>0\). Their parameter-estimation guarantee is a major improvement over earlier polynomial separation requirements. The theorem does not set \(c=0\), and its common known covariance differs from the full unequal-scale formulation.

Qiao and coauthors give a Fourier-based algorithm with stronger separation guarantees in the low-dimensional regime \(d=O(\log k/\log\log k)\). Their general runtime is polynomial in \(k\) multiplied by a function of dimension, separation and accuracy. This does not provide one polynomial bound over the full high-dimensional parameter range.

The 2026 sparse-Fourier method efficiently learns mixtures whose component characteristic functions decay sufficiently slowly. The main theorem explicitly excludes Gaussians. Its combined treatment of slow- and fast-decaying components retains separate separation and runtime dependencies for the latter, so it does not establish the present Gaussian threshold.

COLT 2026 gives substantial improvements for nonspherical centered mixtures and mixtures with identical unknown covariance. The centered result retains a nonpolynomial function of inverse minimum weight, and the equal-covariance result retains a weight-dependent exponent. Neither theorem supplies the fully polynomial growing-component guarantee specified here.
